24--- The *functional style* of programming is founded on simple, everyday
25--- mathematical intuitions: If a program has no side effects, such as reading
26--- or writing files or network packets, then (ignoring efficiency) all we need
27--- to understand about it is how it maps inputs to outputs. That is, we can
28--- think of it as just a concrete means for computing a mathematical function.
29--- This direct connection between programs and simple mathematical objects
30--- supports both formal correctness proofs and sound informal reasoning about
31--- program behavior. This is one sense of the word "functional" in "functional
32--- programming."
33-
34--- The other sense in which functional programming is "functional" is that it
35--- emphasizes the use of functions as *first-class* values -- i.e., values
36--- that can be passed as arguments to other functions, returned as results,
37--- included in data structures, etc. The recognition that functions can be
38--- treated as data gives rise to a host of useful and powerful programming
39--- idioms.
5+-- The *functional style* of programming is founded on simple mathematical
6+-- intuitions: A program is essentially a concrete means for computing a
7+-- mathematical function, which just maps inputs to outputs. Even when
8+-- programs have side effects, such as reading or writing files or network
9+-- packets, these side effects can be given a mathematical characterization
10+-- (such as through the use of monads). This connection between programs and
11+-- mathematical functions makes it possible to reason both precisely and
12+-- formally about a program's behavior, i.e., to *prove properties* about
13+-- programs.
14+
15+-- This functional style is one sense of the word "functional" in "functional
16+-- programming." The other sense is that it emphasizes the use of functions as
17+-- *first-class* values — i.e., values that can be passed as arguments to
18+-- other functions, returned as results, included in data structures, etc. The
19+-- recognition that functions can be treated as data gives rise to a host of
20+-- useful and powerful programming idioms.

409+-- ### Aside: Unicode in Lean
410+
411+-- Note that `∀` and `⊢` are unicode symbols, not a simple ASCII characters.
412+-- The Lean Extension for VS Code provides convenient shortcuts for entering
413+-- such symbols. Simply type `\` (backslash) followed by the name of the
414+-- symbol (the "shortcode"), and the extension will automatically replace it
415+-- with the actual symbol. For example, typing `\all` or `\forall` will
416+-- produce `∀` and `\->` or `\to` will produce `→`. To find out what backslash

869+-- structure starting from the old one.

10781083 -- ### The `rewrite` tactic
10791084 
1080--- As we saw above, the tactic that tells Lean to rewrite (part of) a goal or
1081--- hypothesis based on a rule is called `rewrite`. Given the rule `add_zero`,
1082--- which states that `n + zero` is equal to `n` for any `n`, we can replace
1083--- any `n + zero` in our proof with `n` via `rewrite [add_zero]`.
1084-
1085--- The `rewrite` tactic takes its argument(s) in square brackets.
1085+-- The `rewrite` tactic tells Lean to rewrite (part of) a goal or hypothesis
1086+-- based on a rule (or rules), given in square brackets. For example, given
1087+-- the rule `add_zero`, which states that `n + zero` is equal to `n` for any
1088+-- `n`, we can replace any `n + zero` in our proof with `n` via
1089+-- `rewrite [add_zero]`.
10861090 
10871091 -- ### The `rfl` tactic
10881092 
10891093 -- The `rfl` tactic closes a goal of the shape `a = a`, for any `a`. It checks
1090--- that both sides of the equality are *definitionally equal* -- that is, that
1094+-- that both sides of the equality are *definitionally equal* — that is, that
10911095 -- they reduce to the same term. (So, in particular, a term is always
10921096 -- definitionally equal to itself.)

11201124 -- ### Irreducibility, Rewriting, and Proof Engineering
11211125 
11221126 -- Lean, like any other programming language, has conventions and best
1123--- practices for writing good software. In object-oriented programming, for
1124--- example, it is considered good practice not to access the fields of an
1125--- object directly, but instead to use getter and setter methods. This helps

16941616 
16951617 -- Lean has a very flexible notation system. Operators like `+` and `*` are
16961618 -- defined with specified precedence and associativity. For example, `+` has
16971619 -- precedence 65 and is left-associative, while `*` has precedence 70 and is
1698--- also left-associative. This means that `1+2*3*4` is parsed as
1699--- `1+((2*3)*4)`.
1620+-- also left-associative. This means that `1 + 2 * 3 * 4` is parsed as
1621+-- `1 + ((2 * 3) * 4)`.
17001622 
17011623 -- You can define custom notation using the `notation`, `infixl`, `infixr`,
17021624 -- `prefix`, and `postfix` commands.
17041626 -- Lean handles notation scoping through namespaces and *type classes*. The
17051627 -- numeric literal `3` can be interpreted as `Nat`, `Int`, `Float`, etc.,
17061628 -- depending on the expected type, thanks to Lean's `OfNat` type class. We
1707--- will explain type classes in more detail in the `Typeclasses` chapter,
1708--- found in `Typeclasses.lean`.

17251642 -- terminates. Specifically, it checks that one of the parameters is

1727--- the definition is made on an argument that is smaller than the original

1729--- `even` is the variable `n'`. Because of our pattern match, we know that `n`
1730--- is equal to `succ (succ n')`, and therefore that `n'` is smaller than `n`.
1731--- This makes `n'` an acceptable argument to `even` for Lean's termination

21---     `HIDE: MRC 3/22: I offer a few remarks. I'm putting them here, above
22---     the BCP'21 comment, not to say that they are in any way more
23---     important; rather, just to preserve some chronological legibility.
24---
25---     - This chapter is an outlier in length. It now has the maximum line
26---       length (in the FULL version) of any chapter in LF, at about 2300
27---       LoC. That's a z-score of about 1.75 for the "blue arrow" chapters
28---       in the dependency diagram.
29---
30---     - This chapter has 39 exercises, of which 25 (!) are optional.
31---
32---     - The running example of evenness is known to be uncompelling
33---       because it is representable without inductively-defined
34---       propositions. There do exist compelling examples:
35---
36---       + Functions like `factorial` whose "natural" definitions are not
37---         structurally recursive. [Coq'Art 8.4]  [BCP 25: FWIW, I don't
38---         find the "natural" definition of factorial suitable for present
39---         purposes: the reasons it is better and more natural than a
40---         simple fixpoint seem rather subtle.]
41---
42---       + Partial functions.
43---
44---       + Relations (that are not strictly functions).
45---
46---     I have a couple of personal opinions based on those observations:
47---
48---     - I favor BCP'21's "path 1" of de-emphasizing (to the extent
49---       perhaps of eliminating) evenness.
50---
51---     - I favor re-factoring this chapter into two files, with a main
52---       (blue) path that covers the essentials without cluttering
53---       optional exercises throughout the file.`
54---
55---     HIDE: BCP '21: This chapter has been the subject of a lot of discussion
56---     over the past couple of years, with lots of people expressing
57---     dissatisfaction with the use of evenness as a main example. In this
58---     revision, I have attempted a compromise: keeping evenness as the
59---     running example (because, aside from the artificiality of the example,
60---     it is pretty well polished) but preceding it with short discussions of
61---     several better-motivated examples.
62---
63---     I'm not yet convinced that this goes far enough, though (I was not
64---     satisfied with my lecture on this part of the chapter, even after
65---     adding these examples, though I did do some further streamlining
66---     afterward and there are some further opportunities for streamlining --
67---     perhaps enough to make the present treatment palatible). I see three
68---     possible paths forward:
69---
70---     - 1. Choose a better example and simply replace all the even stuff. (But
71---          which one is better? I don't think we've found it yet.)
72---
73---     - 2. Mix and match -- use different examples from the top of the chapter to
74---          make different points.
75---
76---     - 3. Leave the examples as-is but streamline as much as possible so we don't
77---          get stuck in them.
78---
79---     Here, for reference, is the whole discussion from before:
80---
81---     -----------------
82---
83---     CH: In my Lyon course it became obvious to pretty much everyone that
84---     the inductive definition of evenness that this chapter uses
85---     intensiviely is so silly and artificial that it makes understanding
86---     very hard for most students. There's zero need to define evenness
87---     inductively, when `∃ k, n = 2*k` does the job fine, so inductive
88---     propositions seem to students not something useful, but just
89---     self-inflicted pain. All the inductive propositions, up to subsequences
90---     and the matching on Regular Expressions at the end, have this useless
91---     self-inflicted pain flavour. So I returned to this the following
92---     morning and showed to the students how to define reflexive-transitive
93---     closure as an inductive relation, and afterwards the were able to
94---     follow much better. The code I quickly hacked up for this is at:
95---     https://prosecco.gforge.inria.fr/personal/hritcu/teaching/lyon2019/Multi.v
96---
97---     BCP: Yes, this chapter needs a revamp! For the moment I am going to
98---     just add a couple of sentences to the opening sequence below, to warn
99---     students about this potential confusion. Moving forward, I wonder
100---     whether something like ordered binary trees would be a simple enough
101---     running example.
102---
103---     BCP 20: I remain puzzled by what is the really right example for this
104---     chapter. Ordered trees (and sorted lists) don't feel quite right
105---     because students might think we should define them with Fixpoint, not
106---     inductive. APT 21: Ordered trees are also surprisingly complex to
107---     describe (see VFA/SearchTree.v). Maybe Permutations would be be a good
108---     choice? The only problem is convincing students that the standard Lean
109---     inductive definition is actually correct (see VFA/Perm.v)!
110---
111---     We should also think about how to make the material flow better between
112---     this chapter and ProofObjects. When lecturing about this one I ended up
113---     introducing a lot of the concepts from that one.
114---
115---     --------
116---
117---     LATER: BCP 19: After lecturing on the first part of this chapter, I'm
118---     afraid I have to agree that the Ev / even / evenb stuff is a total
119---     mess. Besides the "why are there so many definitions of evenness?"
120---     problem, evenness is just not a very natural inductively defined
121---     proposition as a first example, because we already have so many
122---     intuitions about what evenness is, and they clash with the new
123---     definition.
124---
125---     So what to do?
126---
127---     An early version of this chapter, years ago, used a completely
128---     artificial inductively defined property of numbers (0 is beautiful,
129---     twice a beautiful number is beautiful, etc.). We could consider going
130---     back to that. Or perhaps there is a more natural example, either
131---     involving numbers or perhaps using some other inductive structure like
132---     lists or binary trees. Not sure what's best.
133---
134---     A related issue is that later chapters (ProofObjects, IndPrinciples)
135---     also rely heavily on this example. Sigh.
136---
137---     BCP 20: Tried to sort this out a bit better by renaming the
138---     propositional definition from `Ev` to `eveni`, for symmetry with
139---     `evenb`, and renaming the definition that says "a number is even if it
140---     is twice something" to `evend`. What do people think of this?
141---
142---     BCP 20 update: In parallel, APT tried to sort it out a different way;
143---     his is more consistent with the standard library, so let's try to go
144---     with that one consistently...

453409 -- The question has challenged philosophers for millennia, but a rough and
454410 -- ready answer could be this: A proof of a mathematical proposition `P` is a
455--- written (or spoken) text that instills in the reader (or hearer) the
456--- certainty that `P` is true — an unassailable argument for the truth of `P`.
457--- That is, a proof is an act of communication.
411+-- text that instills in the reader the certainty that `P` is true. That is, a
412+-- proof is an act of *communication*.
458413 
459414 -- Acts of communication may involve different sorts of readers. On one hand,
460415 -- the "reader" can be a program like Lean, in which case the "belief" that is
468423 -- clearly specified. A "valid" proof is one that makes the reader believe
469424 -- `P`. But the same proof may be read by many different readers, some of whom
470425 -- may be convinced by a particular way of phrasing the argument, while others
471--- may not be. Some readers may be particularly pedantic, inexperienced, or
472--- just plain thick-headed; the only way to convince them will be to make the
473--- argument in painstaking detail. Other readers, more familiar in the area,
474--- may find all this detail so overwhelming that they lose the overall thread;
475--- all they want is to be told the main ideas, since it is easier for them to
476--- fill in the details for themselves than to wade through a written
477--- presentation of them. Ultimately, there is no universal standard, because
478--- there is no single way of writing an informal proof that will convince
479--- every conceivable reader.
426+-- may not be. Some readers may be particularly inexperienced or just plain
427+-- thick-headed; the only way to convince them will be to make the argument in
428+-- painstaking detail. Other readers, more familiar in the area, may find all
429+-- this detail so overwhelming that they lose the overall thread; all they
430+-- want is to be told the main ideas, since it is easier for them to fill in
431+-- the details for themselves than to wade through a written presentation of
432+-- them. Ultimately, there is no universal standard, because there is no
433+-- single way of writing an informal proof that will convince every
434+-- conceivable reader.

481436 -- In practice, however, mathematicians have developed a rich set of
482437 -- conventions and idioms for writing about complex mathematical objects that
549504 -- generates the same sub-goals, in the same order, as the bullet points that
550505 -- a mathematician would usually write. But there are significant differences
551506 -- of detail: the formal proof is much more explicit in some ways (e.g., the
552--- use of `rfl`) but much less explicit in others (in particular, the "proof
553--- state" at any given point in the Lean proof is completely implicit, whereas
554--- the informal proof reminds the reader several times where things stand).

1009--- The reason is that the identifier `add_comm` actually refers to a *proof
1010--- object* -- a logical derivation establishing the truth of the statement
1011--- `∀ n m, n + m = m + n`. The type of this object is the proposition that it
1012--- is a proof of.

986+-- *proof object* — a logical derivation establishing the truth of the
987+-- statement `∀ n m : Nat, n + m = m + n`. The type of this object is the
988+-- proposition that it is a proof of.

3+-- # Postscript
4+
5+-- Congratulations: We've made it to the end of *Logical Foundations*!
6+
7+-- ## Looking Back
8+
9+-- We've covered quite a bit of ground so far. Here's a quick review...
10+
11+-- - *Functional programming*:
12+
13+--   - "declarative" programming style (recursion over immutable data structures,
14+--     rather than looping over mutable arrays or pointer structures)
15+
16+--   - higher-order functions
17+
18+--   - polymorphism
19+
20+-- - *Logic*, the mathematical basis for software engineering:
21+
22+-- logic                        calculus
23+-- --------------------   ~   ----------------------------
24+-- software engineering       mechanical/civil engineering
25+
26+-- - inductively defined sets and relations
27+-- - inductive proofs
28+-- - proof objects
29+
30+-- - *Lean*, an industrial-strength proof assistant
31+-- - functional core language
32+-- - core tactics
33+-- - automation
34+
35+-- ## Looking Forward
36+
37+-- OLD: If what you've seen so far has whetted your interest, you have several
38+-- choices for further reading in later volumes of the *Software Foundations*
39+-- series. Some of these are intended to be accessible to readers immediately
40+-- after finishing *Logical Foundations*; others require a few chapters from
41+-- Volume 2, *Programming Language Foundations*. The Preface chapter in each
42+-- volume gives details about prerequisites.
43+
44+-- FINISH: As of August 2026, there are two more volumes written in Lean.
45+
46+-- *Hoare Logic*: This short volume describes one of the primary methods for
47+-- reasoning about *imperative* programs- programs with state and mutation,
48+-- like C++, Java, C, and Assembly- in a pure logic like Lean's. This method,
49+-- called *Hoare Logic*, is embeddable into Lean's type system and is a
50+-- powerful tool for determining the correct behavior of imperative code.
51+-- Since most of the code in the wild today is imperative, this technique is
52+-- both well-established and popular among industry professionals who analyze
53+-- and fortify the correctness of systems.
54+
55+-- *Type Systems*: Another tool for reasoning about the correctness of a
56+-- program is a *type system*. You have interacted thoroughly with Lean's rich
57+-- type system, which is one of the most complex in a modern programming
58+-- language. Most languages have type systems that are far less complex, but
59+-- which still provide incredibly useful guardrails against ill-behaved
60+-- programs. In this volume you will explore how to read, analyze, and design
61+-- type systems in a proof assistant.
62+
63+-- ## Resources
64+
65+-- Here are some other good places to learn more...
66+
67+-- - This book includes some optional chapters covering topics that you may find
68+--   useful. Take a look at the #<a href="toc.html">#table of contents#</a># and
69+--   the #<a href="deps.html">#chapter dependency diagram#</a># to find them.
70+
71+-- - For questions about Rocq, the `#coq` area of Stack Overflow
72+--   (<https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/coq>) is an excellent
73+--   community resource.
74+
75+-- - Here are some great books on functional programming
76+
77+--   - Learn You a Haskell for Great Good, by Miran Lipovaca Lipovaca 2011.
78+
79+--   - Real World Haskell, by Bryan O'Sullivan, John Goerzen, and Don Stewart
80+--     O'Sullivan 2008
81+
82+--   - ...and many other excellent books on Haskell, OCaml, Scheme, Racket, Scala,
83+--     F sharp, etc., etc.
84+
85+-- - And some further resources for Rocq:
86+
87+--   - Certified Programming with Dependent Types, by Adam Chlipala Chlipala 2013.
88+
89+--   - Interactive Theorem Proving and Program Development: Coq'Art: The Calculus
90+--     of Inductive Constructions, by Yves Bertot and Pierre Casteran Bertot 2004.
91+
92+-- - If you're interested in real-world applications of formal verification to
93+--   critical software, see the Postscript chapter of *Programming Language
94+--   Foundations*.
95+
96+-- - For applications of Rocq in building verified systems, the lectures and
97+--   course materials for the 2017 DeepSpec Summer School are a great resource.
98+--   <https://deepspec.org/event/dsss17/index.html>

5+-- ## Welcome
6+
7+-- This is the entry point to a series of electronic textbooks on various
8+-- aspects of *Software Foundations*, the mathematical underpinnings of
9+-- reliable software. Topics in the series include basic concepts of logic,
10+-- functional programming, computer-assisted theorem proving, operational
11+-- semantics, logics and techniques for reasoning about programs, static type
12+-- systems, property-based random testing, and verification of practical C
13+-- code. The exposition is intended for a broad range of readers, from
14+-- advanced undergraduates to PhD students and researchers. No specific
15+-- background in logic or programming languages is assumed, though a degree of
16+-- mathematical maturity will be helpful.
17+
18+-- The principal novelty of the series is that it is one hundred percent
19+-- formalized and machine-checked: each text is literally a script for Lean.
20+-- The books are intended to be read alongside (or inside) an interactive
21+-- session with Lean. All the details in the text are fully formalized in
22+-- Lean, and almost all of the exercises are designed to be worked using Lean.
23+
24+-- This book, *Logical Foundations in Lean*, lays groundwork for the others,
25+-- introducing the reader to the basic ideas of functional programming, formal
26+-- logic, and Lean itself.
27+
28+-- ## Overview
29+
30+-- Building reliable software is hard -- really hard. The scale and complexity
31+-- of modern systems, the number of people involved, and the range of demands
32+-- placed on them make it challenging to build software that is even
33+-- more-or-less correct, much less 100% correct. At the same time, the
34+-- increasing degree to which information processing is woven into every
35+-- aspect of society greatly amplifies the cost of bugs and insecurities.
36+
37+-- Computer scientists and software engineers have responded to these
38+-- challenges with a host of techniques for improving software reliability,
39+-- ranging from recommendations about managing software projects teams (e.g.,
40+-- extreme programming) to design philosophies for libraries (e.g.,
41+-- model-view-controller, publish-subscribe, etc.) and whole programming
42+-- languages (e.g., object-oriented programming, functional programming, ...)
43+-- to mathematical techniques for specifying and reasoning about properties of
44+-- software and tools for helping validate these properties. The *Software
45+-- Foundations* books are focused on this last set of tools.
46+
47+-- The present volume weaves together three conceptual threads:
48+
49+-- - basic tools from *logic* for making and justifying precise claims about
50+--   programs;
51+
52+-- - the use of *provers* (or *proof assistants*) to construct rigorous logical
53+--   arguments;
54+
55+-- - *functional programming*, both as a programming method that simplifies
56+--   reasoning about programs and as a bridge between programming and logic.
57+
58+-- ### Logic
59+
60+-- Logic is the field of study whose subject matter is *proofs* --
61+-- unassailable arguments for the truth of particular propositions. Volumes
62+-- have been written about the central role of logic in computer science.
63+-- Manna and Waldinger called it "the calculus of computer science," while
64+-- Halpern et al.'s paper *On the Unusual Effectiveness of Logic in Computer
65+-- Science* catalogs scores of ways in which logic offers critical tools and
66+-- insights. Indeed, they observe that, "As a matter of fact, logic has turned
67+-- out to be significantly more effective in computer science than it has been
68+-- in mathematics. This is quite remarkable, especially since much of the
69+-- impetus for the development of logic during the past one hundred years came
70+-- from mathematics."
71+
72+-- In particular, the fundamental tools of *inductive proof* are ubiquitous
73+-- across computer science. You have surely seen them before, perhaps in a
74+-- course on discrete math or analysis of algorithms, but in this book we will
75+-- examine them more deeply than you have probably done so far.
76+
77+-- ### Proof Assistants
78+
79+-- The flow of ideas between logic and computer science over the years has run
80+-- in both directions, with CS also making contributions to logic. One of
81+-- these has been the development of software tools for helping construct and
82+-- validate proofs of logical statements. These tools fall into two broad
83+-- categories:
84+
85+-- - *Automated theorem provers* provide "push-button" operation: you give them
86+--   a proposition and they return either *true* or *false* (or, sometimes,
87+--   *don't know: ran out of time*). Although their reasoning capabilities are
88+--   limited, they have matured tremendously in recent decades and are used now
89+--   in a multitude of settings. Examples of such tools include SAT solvers, SMT
90+--   solvers, and model checkers.
91+
92+-- - *Proof assistants* — or just *provers* — are hybrid tools that automate the
93+--   more routine aspects of creating proofs while depending on human guidance
94+--   for more difficult aspects. Widely used proof assistants include Isabelle,
95+--   Agda, Twelf, ACL2, PVS, F*, HOL4, Rocq, and Lean, among many others.
96+
97+-- This course is based around Lean, a proof assistant that has been under
98+-- development since 2013 and has attracted a large and active community of
99+-- users in both research and at companies like DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic,
100+-- MSR, and AWS.
101+
102+-- Lean provides a rich environment for interactive development of
103+-- machine-checked formal reasoning. The kernel of the Lean system is a simple
104+-- proof-checker, which guarantees that only correct deduction steps are ever
105+-- performed. On top of this kernel, the Lean environment provides high-level
106+-- facilities for proof development, including a large library of common
107+-- definitions and lemmas, powerful tactics for constructing complex proofs
108+-- semi-automatically, and a highly extensible system for defining new
109+-- proof-automation tactics and notations for specific situations.
110+
111+-- Lean and its relatives have become a critical enablers for a huge variety
112+-- of work across computer science and mathematics:
113+
114+-- - As a *platform for modeling programming languages*, they have become
115+--   standard tools for researchers who need to describe and reason about
116+--   complex language definitions. They have been used, for example, to check
117+--   the security of the JavaCard platform, obtaining the highest level of
118+--   common criteria certification, and for formal specifications of the x86 and
119+--   LLVM instruction sets and programming languages such as C.
120+
121+-- - As *environments for developing formally certified software and hardware*,
122+--   they been used, for example, to build CompCert, a fully-verified optimizing
123+--   compiler for C, and CertiKOS, a fully verified hypervisor, for proving the
124+--   correctness of subtle algorithms involving floating point numbers, and as
125+--   the basis for CertiCrypt, FCF, and SSProve, which are frameworks for
126+--   proving cryptographic algorithms secure. They are also being used to build
127+--   verified implementations of the open-source RISC-V processor architecture.
128+
129+-- - As *proof assistants for mathematics*, they have been used to validate and
130+--   help develop a number of important results. For example, the ability to
131+--   include complex computations inside proofs made it possible to develop the
132+--   first formally verified proof of the 4-color theorem. This proof had
133+--   previously been controversial among mathematicians because it required
134+--   checking a large number of configurations using a program. More recently,
135+--   an even more massive effort led to a formalization of the Feit-Thompson
136+--   Theorem, the first major step in the classification of finite simple
137+--   groups.
138+
139+-- ### Functional Programming
140+
141+-- *Functional programming* refers both to a collection of idioms that can be
142+-- used in almost any programming language and to a family of languages
143+-- designed to foreground these idioms, including Haskell, OCaml, Standard ML,
144+-- F##, Scala, Scheme, Racket, Common Lisp, Clojure, Erlang, F*, and Lean
145+-- itself.
146+
147+-- Functional programming has been developed over many decades — indeed, its
148+-- roots go back to Church's lambda-calculus from the 1930s, well *before* the
149+-- first electronic computers! But since the early '90s it has enjoyed a surge
150+-- of interest among both software engineers and language designers.
151+
152+-- The most basic tenet of functional programming is that, whenever possible,
153+-- computation should be *pure*, in the sense that the only effect of
154+-- execution should be to produce a result: it should be free from *side
155+-- effects* such as I/O, assignments to mutable variables, redirecting
156+-- pointers, etc. For example, whereas an *imperative* sorting function might
157+-- take a list of numbers and rearrange its pointers to put the list in order,
158+-- a pure sorting function would take the original list and return a fresh
159+-- list containing the same numbers in sorted order.
160+
161+-- A significant benefit of this style of programming is that it makes
162+-- programs easier to understand and reason about. If every operation on a
163+-- data structure yields a new data structure, leaving the old one intact,
164+-- then there is no need to worry about how that structure is being shared and
165+-- whether a change by one part of the program might break an invariant relied
166+-- on by another part of the program. These considerations are particularly
167+-- critical in concurrent systems, where every piece of mutable state shared
168+-- between threads is a potential source of pernicious bugs.
169+
170+-- Another reason for the popularity of functional programming is related to
171+-- the first: functional programs are often much easier to parallelize and
172+-- physically distribute than their imperative counterparts. If running a
173+-- computation has no effect other than producing a result, then it does not
174+-- matter *where* it is run. Similarly, if a data structure is never modified
175+-- destructively, it can be copied freely, across cores or across the network.
176+-- Indeed, the "Map-Reduce" idiom, which lies at the heart of massively
177+-- distributed query processors like Hadoop and is used by Google to index the
178+-- entire web, is a classic example of functional programming.
179+
180+-- For purposes of these books, functional programming has yet another
181+-- significant attraction: it serves as a bridge between logic and computer
182+-- science. Indeed, Lean itself can be viewed as a combination of a small but
183+-- extremely expressive functional programming language and a set of tools for
184+-- stating and proving logical assertions. Moreover, when we come to look more
185+-- closely, we find that these two sides of Lean are actually aspects of the
186+-- very same underlying machinery -- i.e., *proofs are programs*.
187+
188+-- ### Further Reading
189+
190+-- This text is intended to be self contained, but readers looking for a
191+-- deeper treatment of particular topics will find some suggestions for
192+-- further reading in the Postscript chapter.
193+
194+-- ## Practicalities
195+
196+-- ### System Requirements
197+
198+-- Lean runs on Windows, Linux, and MacOS. The files in this book have been
199+-- tested with Lean version `4.32.0`.
200+
201+-- ### Installation
202+
203+-- The Visual Studio Code IDE is the recommended platform for using Lean.
204+
205+-- - Install VS Code if needed
206+
207+-- - From the Extensions tab of VS Code, install the Lean 4 extension
208+
209+-- - Clone the [SF-in-Lean](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean) git repo and
210+--   open it in VS Code
211+
212+-- - The first time you open a Lean file, the extension will offer to install
213+--   Lean itself; accept, and it will fetch the version this book needs
214+
215+-- - Wait for Lean to build the project (it takes a few minutes)
216+
217+-- ### Exercises
218+
219+-- Each chapter includes numerous exercises. Each is marked with a "star
220+-- rating," which can be interpreted as follows:
221+
222+-- - One star: easy exercises that underscore points in the text and that, for
223+--   most readers, should take only a minute or two. Get in the habit of working
224+--   these as you reach them.
225+
226+-- - Two stars: straightforward exercises (five or ten minutes).
227+
228+-- - Three stars: exercises requiring a bit of thought (ten minutes to half an
229+--   hour).
230+
231+-- - Four and five stars: more difficult exercises (half an hour and up).
232+
233+-- Those using SF in a classroom setting should note that the autograder
234+-- assigns extra points to harder exercises:
235+
236+-- 1 star  = 1 point
237+-- 2 stars = 2 points
238+-- 3 stars = 3 points
239+-- 4 stars = 6 points
240+-- 5 stars = 10 points
241+
242+-- Some exercises are marked "advanced," and some are marked "optional." Doing
243+-- just the non-optional, non-advanced exercises should provide good coverage
244+-- of the core material. Optional exercises provide a bit of extra practice
245+-- with key concepts and introduce secondary themes that may be of interest to
246+-- some readers. Advanced exercises offer an extra challenge and a deeper cut
247+-- at the ideas.
248+
249+-- ### Citation Format
250+
251+-- If you want to refer to this volume in your own writing, please do so as
252+-- follows:
253+
254+-- @book            {SFL:1,
255+-- author       =   {Mike Hicks and Benjamin C. Pierce and the SF-in-Lean team},
256+-- title        =   "Logical Foundations",
257+-- series       =   "Software Foundations in Lean",
258+-- volume       =   "1",
259+-- year         =   "2026",
260+-- publisher    =   "Electronic textbook",
261+-- note         =   {Version 0.1.0, \URL<https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean>}
262+-- }
263+
264+-- ## For Potential Contributors
265+
266+-- If you find things you'd like to help add or improve, your contributions
267+-- are welcome! To get started, clone the [SF-in-Lean git
268+-- repo](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean) and have a look at
269+-- `ALPHATESTERS.md`.
270+
271+-- ## For Instructors
272+
273+-- A large compendium of exams from many offerings of CIS5000 ("Software
274+-- Foundations") at the University of Pennsylvania can be found at
275+-- <https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis5000/current/exams/index.html>. Until 2026,
276+-- the course was offered in Rocq, but the ideas behind the problems are still
277+-- relevant.
278+
279+-- ## Acknowledgements
280+
281+-- See `ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS.md` in the [SF-in-Lean git
282+-- repo](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean).
283+

462+-- Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean when the same

467+-- `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass `MyGetElem` is a simpler
468+-- version of the standard library's `GetElem` typeclass, which has many
469+-- instances such as `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it to
470+-- illustrate the notation-as-typeclass approach.
